extracted.intended_audience: academic authors seeking freelance copyediting for articles or books
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for academics on when to hire a freelance copyeditor, how to prepare a manuscript, how to choose the type of edit and an editor, expected costs and pace, and how to work with the editor (including trial edits for books).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of copyediting
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyediting is the task of correcting a manuscript from an author by catching grammar and spelling errors, standardizing style and documentation, and improving clarity and flow, all while not introducing errors or changing the author’s meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No machine can perform the full set of decisions a human copyeditor makes. Copyediting is more intensive and skillful than basic proofreading; it may include many small decisions every minute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of proofreading
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofreading is correcting a print-ready document from the publisher. Frequently, people without training use the word proofreading to refer to a light edit (correcting only basic errors) and copyediting to refer to a heavy edit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofreading is usually less intensive and takes less skill than copyediting. Many beginners start as proofreaders and later move on to copyediting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected hourly rates and editing speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Few academic copyeditors charge less than $35/hour; good editors charge at least $50/hour and generally $75–$85/hour. Copyeditors edit from 2 to 5 pages an hour; average rate is 4 pages (1,000 words) per hour. Manuscripts with many problems may slow to 1 page/hour or 0.5 page/hour; very clean manuscripts may go as fast as 8 pages/hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setting up to edit a manuscript takes 2–3 hours (amortized across a book). Use these numbers to estimate time and cost for budgeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost examples and budgeting method
rubrics_metrics.description: A 30-page article may cost as much as $2,000; expect to pay at least $500 for an article. A full-length 500-page book needing a lot of editing could cost up to $17,500 (if $35/hour and 1 hour/page), but most authors will likely spend $4,000–$5,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To estimate cost: count total words, divide by 250 to get pages, then divide pages by 4 (pages/hour) and multiply by the hourly rate. Fix what you can first to avoid paying for easy fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who should consider hiring a copyeditor
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone can benefit from copyediting. Authors who have never had a professional copyedit, non-native English speakers, and those told by instructors or colleagues that their work could benefit from copyediting should hire one. If grammar and awkward constructions impair clarity, hire a copyeditor before submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider copyediting as an investment: a well-edited article is likelier to succeed in the submission process and can contribute to career advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare your manuscript before hiring
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should clean the manuscript before sending it to a copyeditor: spell-check footnotes, standardize references, and fix easily correctable issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doing what you can yourself saves money. Precisely count pages (total electronic word count divided by 250) to avoid surprises when estimating cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to find and how to choose a copyeditor
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask colleagues for recommendations or use directories such as the Editorial Freelancers Association (EFA) searchable by skill, subject specialty, and location; consider services like Mafoko Manuscript Services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick an academic copyeditor familiar with your field and its conventions. Check summaries of members' freelance services and contact information; prefer editors with relevant subject expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give clear instructions about desired edit type
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four main kinds of editing: technical editing, style editing, correlation editing, and substantive editing. Tell the copyeditor which kind(s) of edit you want.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive editing is most time-consuming and valuable. If you struggle with grammar ask for a technical edit plus substantive edit; if confident in grammar, substantive alone may suffice. Style editing can be requested if you must meet publisher format, but authors can sometimes do this themselves to save money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical editing (specific tasks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical editing involves correcting misspellings, subject-verb agreement problems, incorrect verb tense, unnecessary or missing commas, unmarked em-dashes/en-dashes, dangling or misplaced modifiers, pronoun-antecedent agreement problems, misused words (e.g., effect vs. affect), split or fused sentences, sentence fragments, faulty parallel construction, figures that don’t total in charts/tables, incorrect dates, and omitted or repeated words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical editing focuses on sentence-level correctness and basic mechanics; it's appropriate when grammar and usage need attention but not large-scale restructuring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style editing (standardization tasks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style editing standardizes a text according to a particular manual of style (e.g., Chicago, APA, MLA, AP). It covers matters where there is no absolute right or wrong but consistency is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style editing includes standardizing heads, bibliography title formats, single vs double quotes, serial commas, numbers, acronyms, compound words, extracts, italics, note numbers, documentation/references style, and illustrations. Use the appropriate style manual for your discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation editing (cross-checking related parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlation editing checks related parts of the manuscript against each other: cross-references to pages, tables, charts, maps, captions, endnotes, subheads; comparing citations in text with the references list; checking titles and authors against the table of contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is essential in academic work and often overlooked by editors who work mainly on novels or newspapers; ensure the copyeditor will perform these crosschecks for academic manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive editing (content, structure, and clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive editing (content editing) involves improving logic and clarity and addressing larger problems of structure and organization. Tasks include replacing passive voice with active voice, varying repeated verbs, clarifying subordinate material with dashes/parentheses, reducing adjective strings, replacing indefinite pronouns with clear nouns, reducing use of a pet word/phrase, removing racist/sexist connotations, defining special terms on first use, cutting wordy sentences, making parallel forms, straightening out logic and connections, noting awkward phrasing, adding transitions, deleting irrelevant material or moving it to footnotes, moving misplaced paragraphs, deleting repeated paragraphs, adding subheads, cutting long footnotes, adjusting titles, suggesting additional citation or research, suggesting illustrations, noting absence of introduction/conclusion, flagging where title does not match content, identifying tangled or absent arguments, and suggesting where the argument could be strengthened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive editing is broad and can change the manuscript's organization and argumentation; it is the most time-consuming and valuable edit for improving clarity and persuasiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layout preparation editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Layout preparation editing involves marking or coding the manuscript for the layout artist so parts of the text (heads, tables, footnote references, etc.) are clear for design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes marking/coding heads and subheads, references in the text to tables/charts/figures/maps/appendixes/footnotes, dashes (en and em), ellipses, and specifying placement of tables and illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissions and rights-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissions involves asking for permission to reprint previously published tables, charts, graphs, and illustrations. If there are lengthy quotations from a published work that remains under copyright, the copyeditor should remind the author to obtain permission. Special rules apply to reproducing unpublished materials (e.g., diaries, letters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The copyeditor is expected to flag and remind authors about permissions issues; authors should be prepared to obtain necessary permissions for copyrighted or unpublished materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial chapter for book-length projects
rubrics_metrics.description: For book-length manuscripts, have the copyeditor edit one chapter and send it to you for review before proceeding with the rest of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewing the trial chapter lets you assess the editor's work; if the editor finds standard errors you can correct them before sending the rest, potentially saving time and money.
